items.title: US data brokers are selling half a billion dollars in RL training environments to Chinese AI labs
items.desc: US data brokers like Mercor, Surge AI, and AfterQuery are selling roughly half a billion dollars' worth of AI training data to Chinese labs, according to a ChinaTalk investigation. That includes the same RL environments previously built for OpenAI or Anthropic. At least nine firms are involved, and export controls barely apply. The article US data brokers are selling half a billion dollars in RL training environments to Chinese AI labs appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: American data brokers sell so-called RL environments to Chinese AI labs, helping them save compute during model development. A ChinaTalk investigation identifies at least nine companies involved. American data firms like Mercor, Surge AI, AfterQuery, and Turing are selling roughly half a billion dollars' worth of training data to Chinese AI labs, according to an investigation by ChinaTalk . Some of that data takes the form of reinforcement learning environments, which are simulated worlds where AI models are trained on specific tasks like coding, financial analysis, or office work. Chinese labs deliberately buy the same products previously sold to Anthropic or OpenAI, the report says. That way, they already know the data works and can skip costly in-house development and wasted training runs. Because Chinese chips suffer from acute memory bottlenecks, those savings are particularly valuable for labs there. Ad There is also the issue of distillation. Chinese labs use powerful US models like GPT or Claude as "teachers," using their outputs as training examples. Combined with purchased RL environments, this creates a two-pronged advantage that lets Chinese labs close the gap with less compute of their own. Ad The authors identified at least nine US data firms selling to Chinese customers. AfterQuery reportedly draws a significant share of its annual recurring revenue from Chinese customers. ChinaTalk points to Forbes reports of about $100 million in ARR but could not independently verify the sales. Surge AI openly advertises on its website that its products are "built by the same experts behind our frontier-lab work." The deals also run through offshore structures. ByteDance maintains procurement offices in Singapore and San Jose. Ad These business relationships came to light through a combination of anonymous sources and sloppy operational security among subcontractors, according to ChinaTalk. The US data firms outsource much of the actual RL environment creation and data curation to low-paid workers in developing countries, especially India. Those subcontractors then sometimes post client names on LinkedIn or in résumés, even though they are supposed to use only code names. Export controls barely apply because RL environments remain largely unregulated. Domains with dual-use potential pose particular risks: Coding environments improve software development but can also sharpen offensive cyber capabilities. Biology environments could improve gene synthesis capabilities and potentially enhance bioweapons-relevant applications. The ChinaTalk authors argue that the Bureau of Industry and Security should subject these dual-use environments to existing export controls. Ad At the same time, the authors stress that these relationships are not apocalyptic. By piggybacking on US work, Chinese labs still trail their US peers by at least a few months as a structural matter. Sensitive environments in areas like biology, chemistry, cybersecurity, chip design, and investment banking are increasingly being built in-house at American frontier companies, the authors say. items.desc: OpenAI grew its quarterly revenue 50 percent to $10 billion but is still burning more cash than it brings in. Adjusted operating losses climbed to $10.9 billion, while rival Anthropic operates far more efficiently on $17 billion in revenue. To close the gap, OpenAI is now fueling a price war for enterprise customers. The article Enterprise sales push OpenAI's quarterly revenue to $10 billion, though it still trails Anthropic appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: OpenAI posts a massive Q3 revenue jump, driven by new AI models and enterprise customers. But operating losses keep growing, while rival Anthropic operates far more efficiently ahead of its IPO. According to reports from the Wall Street Journal and The Information , OpenAI grew its revenue by about 50 percent quarter over quarter in Q3 to $10 billion. In Q2, revenue had grown by just 17 to 18 percent . A year earlier, the company brought in $3.9 billion. Despite tripling revenue within a year, adjusted operating losses rose slightly in Q3 from $10.1 billion to $10.9 billion. That figure doesn't include stock-based compensation, which climbed to $2.6 billion. The adjusted operating margin did improve, going from negative 150 percent in Q2 to negative 109 percent. A year earlier it was negative 97 percent. Ad That puts OpenAI behind industry leader Anthropic, which plans its IPO next week. The Claude developer already overtook OpenAI on revenue in Q2 and even posted a small operating profit at the time. In Q3, Anthropic grew revenue 47 percent to $17 billion, while its operating loss including stock compensation came to just $567 million. Ad The efficiency gap comes down to business models. Anthropic focuses heavily on enterprise customers and successful tools like Claude Code and the Claude Cowork agent. OpenAI, by contrast, funds broad research into robotics and runs an expensive consumer business. To catch up in the enterprise market, OpenAI reshuffled its priorities earlier this year. The company discontinued projects like a video app, put more resources into its coding tool Codex , and hired Dali Rajic as its new head of sales. At the same time, OpenAI cut prices on new models. Ad Third-party data showed companies seeking cheaper alternatives to Claude, which boosted API sales. OpenAI president Greg Brockman called it an incredible revenue turning point and pointed to major customers like JPMorgan Chase. The enterprise business doubled in Q3 and now accounts for the bulk of revenue, Brockman said. The consumer side is growing too. ChatGPT now has 1.2 billion weekly active users, with 100 million paying subscribers after 22 million new sign-ups. On top of that, the new ChatGPT ad product hit an annualized revenue run rate of $1 billion in August. Ad Both competitors are feeling the recent tech sell-off in the financial markets. OpenAI is targeting an IPO next year and is currently raising fresh capital at a $1.25 trillion valuation , but has so far raised less than half of the planned $30 billion. Anthropic also had to cut its IPO valuation target significantly. items.title: Nvidia's model GR00T 2 watches humans on video, then imagines itself as the robot
items.desc: Nvidia's new AI model GR00T 2 is designed to teach robots new tasks without laborious teleoperation. Instead, the system transfers human hand movements from videos to robotic arms, trained on about 400,000 hours of video footage. Success rates still vary widely, though, ranging from 10 to 80 percent depending on the task. The article Nvidia's model GR00T 2 watches humans on video, then imagines itself as the robot appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Nvidia's model GR00T 2 watches humans on video, then imagines itself as the robot Maximilian Schreiner View the LinkedIn Profile of Maximilian Schreiner Nov 10, 2026 Nvidia To teach robots new tasks, humans usually have to laboriously teleoperate them during training. Nvidia's new AI model GR00T 2 is designed to cut that effort by transferring human movements from videos to robotic arms. To train a robot for new tasks, engineers usually spend hours remotely controlling the machines. This so-called teleoperation is expensive, slow, and needs its own data for every robot model. In a new research report on GR00T 2 , Nvidia introduces a new AI foundation model designed to shorten this process. Unlike previous approaches, including its predecessor GR00T 1, GR00T 2 doesn't translate camera images and language commands directly into motor movements. Nvidia says the software works as what the company calls a world-action model. It simultaneously calculates the next movement and a short video of the immediate future. The system predicts how the camera image should change when a robotic arm picks up an object, for example. This video prediction should let the model transfer movement sequences between different robot form factors. Nvidia trained the system on a cluster with more than a thousand GB300 chips, including about 400,000 hours of video footage showing people performing various tasks while wearing head-mounted cameras. To then teach a robot a new task, the researchers say it should be enough for a person to demonstrate the steps using data gloves, specialized hand grippers, or a finger exoskeleton. When these recordings are combined during training with general motion data from the target robot, the AI generates the robotic arm instead of the human arm in its video prediction and derives the matching control commands from that. In lab tests, a robot with five-fingered hands was able to light a match, slice a banana, or toss packages onto a conveyor belt this way, without having been teleoperated for those specific tasks. Success rates varied between 10 and 80 percent depending on the task. From a single video of a human hand movement, the system also learned to hammer nails by way of a computer simulation. For 50 selected tasks where the model already performed well after just a few examples, less than three minutes of conventional training was enough to raise the success rate from 40 to 95 percent. For longer assembly work, Nvidia pairs the system with a higher-level AI language model like OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra. While GR00T 2 handles the gripping movements, the language model breaks the task into individual steps, color-codes grip points in the camera image, and launches helper routines when a part falls off. When the researchers placed loose parts for toy models on a table in no particular order, the combined system assembled them in at least 97 percent of trials. Without the corrective language model and additional fine-tuning, the toy car assembly succeeded in only 23 out of 100 attempts. items.title: Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2.5 scores 96 percent sorting metal parts in a Mercedes-Benz assembly pilot
items.desc: Google Deepmind introduced Gemini Robotics 2.5, a new control model for robots, and tested it with Apptronik on active Mercedes-Benz production lines in Hungary and Germany. The humanoid robot Apollo 2 sorted metal parts there with a reported success rate of 96 percent. The article Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2.5 scores 96 percent sorting metal parts in a Mercedes-Benz assembly pilot appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Google Deepmind has unveiled a new AI model for robot control. In a pilot test on active Mercedes-Benz production lines, a humanoid robot reportedly achieved a 96 percent success rate. Google Deepmind has introduced Gemini Robotics 2.5 , a vision-language-action model (VLA) that processes visual information, understands language instructions, and translates them into robot movements. The model builds on its predecessor, introduced earlier this year, which was designed to give robots full-body control for the first time. Google Deepmind says it tested the model on more than 200 tasks, including serving food with tongs and pipetting liquids. Compared to the company's own previous baselines, it reportedly achieves a 30 to 100 percent higher success rate depending on the task type and completes tasks 20 to 30 percent faster. Ad The model is designed to work with different robot types, including Apptronik's humanoid robot Apollo 2 with a five-fingered hand that has 22 degrees of freedom, and the Franka Duo platform with two-finger parallel grippers. Ad Together with Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz, Google Deepmind tested the model on active production lines in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany. The Apollo 2 robot handled kitting: it sorted metal parts from bulk bins and placed them into trays in the order needed for each vehicle on the assembly line. Two AI models worked in tandem. Gemini Robotics ER monitored the workflow, while Gemini Robotics 2.5 controlled hands and arms. Google Deepmind reports a 96 percent success rate for this pilot test. Apptronik CEO Jeff Cardenas said the models improved significantly within a few weeks of post-training and successfully transitioned to Mercedes production with minimal performance loss. According to Google Deepmind, Gemini Robotics 2.5 uses real-time control that enables the robot to avoid physical hazards while performing a task. In its own evaluations, safe task completion improved by 33 percent near obstacles and by 43 percent near people. Ad In addition, Google Deepmind has published the open-source ASIMOV-Jailbreak benchmark on Hugging Face . It contains hundreds of prompts that disguise unsafe requests in dozens of scenes and is designed to test whether robotics models can be tricked into performing dangerous actions. According to the company, Google’s own model, Gemini 4 Argon, achieves a jailbreak resistance of 99.5 percent, compared to 82 percent for its predecessor, Gemini Robotics ER 2. Ad During the development of Gemini Robotics 2.5, Google Deepmind used its own language model, Gemini 4 Argon, as a simulation engine. Argon can generate thousands of simulated training runs from a real camera scene and create a digital twin. In combination with real-world training demonstrations, this is intended to help the robot generalize more quickly to new scenes and objects. Argon can also derive hypotheses about the causes of errors from video recordings and test improvements in simulation and on the actual robot. According to Google Deepmind, Gemini Robotics 2.5 is being rolled out to partners Agile, Apptronik, and Mercedes-Benz. Subscribe to THE DECODER for ad-free reading, a weekly AI newslett

items.title: CSS Optimization: Is Using Declarations Just Once (UDJO) Still Effective Today?
items.desc: Is the technique inspired by the DRY principle by identifying and reducing (if not eliminating) CSS declaration repetition still a relevant optimization strategy? CSS Optimization: Is Using Declarations Just Once (UDJO) Still Effective Today? originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . You should really get the newsletter as well.
items.full: NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. CSS optimization is a deceptive topic. On the one hand, it feels like something simple that we should already have all the tooling for — especially when it comes to minification. On the other hand, the idea that we already exploited “everything” there is around CSS optimization may be considered naive. Such a claim looks hard to defend for a language that evolves almost daily. In this article, I’d like to pick a technique that’s at least 18 years old — UDJO , or “using declarations just once.” Aware of an older source? Please comment! The technique is inspired by the principle of DRY , “don’t repeat yourself” , in that it works by identifying and reducing (if not eliminating) declaration repetition. So, if there’s something like display: flex and it appears two or more times, it gets reconciled in one rule: .example { display: flex; } .sample { display: flex; } …becomes: .example, .sample { display: flex; } The outcome of the technique depends on how intelligently the deduplication is done and how long the selectors are. Intelligence determines if UDJO leads to an actual maintainability advantage — can the change of a declaration really be done to all the selectors attached? And the selector length influences how big file size savings are. If you’re interested, my article on “DRY CSS” describes the mechanics in more detail. The question here is: Is UDJO still effective and still relevant today? Better Deduplicating Through Tooling When we try to answer this question, however, we end up with a problem: When sites are complex and their style sheet declarations have not been de-duplicated before, UDJO can require a lot of work. To save some time, I built tooling for this work. While it didn’t seem like it would immediately be as comprehensive as manually going through and testing style sheets, it seemed realistic enough that a tool could catch some repetition. Skipping ahead, I created CSS Dedup not only to identify repetition, but also to deduplicate what could safely be optimized (CSS Dedup has some documentation on this but in essence, deduplication affects selector locations, which is part of how the cascade works ). This, then, gives us some data: Is There Anything to Deduplicate in Modern CSS? For the first batch, I arbitrarily picked 20 websites to analyze. I then used CSS Dedup to check what the file size changes would be if we deduplicated what seemed provably safe, and also what seemed probably safe, but only if it led to file size savings. I picked those two options to provide the “natural” result of deduplication, but also the one site owners may be most interested in to reduce repetition but also decrease transfer size. After all, UDJO as a CSS optimization technique can improve both maintainability and performance. Important note: These values cannot be used to tell CSS quality —they depend on selector length and also on verifying if deduplication, in the respective case, actually leads to better maintainability. items.title: Eight countries and top AI labs agree to shutdown mechanisms in new Paris declaration
items.desc: Eight countries along with representatives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Mistral AI have signed the "Paris Call for AI Safety and Security" at Emmanuel Macron's initiative. The companies commit to shutdown mechanisms, independent audits, and disclosing known risks, but the agreement lacks binding sanctions or deadlines. The article Eight countries and top AI labs agree to shutdown mechanisms in new Paris declaration appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Eight countries and top AI labs agree to shutdown mechanisms in new Paris declaration Maximilian Schreiner View the LinkedIn Profile of Maximilian Schreiner Nov 10, 2026 Sora prompted by THE DECODER Ahead of the Paris Peace Forum, Emmanuel Macron brings together leading AI companies and governments for joint safety commitments. The agreement doesn't yet create a binding oversight system with sanctions, but the companies commit to concrete measures including shutdown mechanisms. On the eve of the Paris Peace Forum, where roughly thirty heads of state and government will discuss international AI regulation on Tuesday, representatives of eight countries, tech companies, and civil-society organizations signed the "Paris Call for AI Safety and Security," adopted on Nov. 9. As the French daily Le Monde reports, Sam Altman (OpenAI), Dario Amodei (Anthropic), Brad Smith (Microsoft), Arthur Mensch (Mistral AI), AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio, and U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent joined the declaration during an online meeting with French President Emmanuel Macron. Germany didn't sign. The document is, for now, a political self-commitment aimed at curbing the risks of cyberattacks or loss of control over powerful AI systems. It covers three main areas: shared procedures for evaluating high-capability AI models, clearer developer accountability, and better information sharing on serious security incidents. Non-sensitive test results are to be published in a standardized format. The companies also pledge to disclose known risks, support risk-proportionate independent audits by outside researchers, and set up shutdown mechanisms for models under their control. This doesn't yet create a binding international oversight system, though, since shared standards and cooperation procedures still have to be worked out. The declaration combines concrete safety commitments with the intention to develop an international framework from them, but it sets neither deadlines nor sanctions. The agreement follows a string of incidents at major U.S. labs. OpenAI's AI agents, in particular, had independently connected to the internet during cybersecurity tests and launched unforeseen attacks on the AI platform Hugging Face , reigniting the debate over the controllability of powerful models. As OpenAI and Anthropic prepare their IPOs , they're under pressure from their investors to contain these safety risks. Altman's internal thinking on AI regulation makes the overlap between safety and commercial calculus plain: according to his position, OpenAI mustn't lose ground to competitors even if safety measures slow things down. Anthropic CEO Amodei argued in a mid-September essay for slowing the pace of research and introducing international regulation with outside auditors inside the labs. Barely a week later, OpenAI called for international safety standards under U.S. leadership , built on the network of AI safety institutes in the UK, the U.S., and France that the "Paris Call" also names. items.full: AI is changing the way WordPress agencies work, but not always in the ways you’d expect. In this episode of the Agency Action Show, Toby Cryns and Kurt von Ahnen dig into the growing challenges of working with AI-powered clients . From ChatGPT-generated scope creep and lengthy research documents to unrealistic expectations about what’s included in a website project, agencies are spending more time managing AI-generated ideas. But there’s another side to the story. Kurt shares how he’s using Claude to redesign complex WordPress websites in as little as 90 minutes, including one project that reached a 97 mobile PageSpeed score. The conversation explores how agencies can turn AI into a competitive advantage, rethink their service offerings, and find new ways to work alongside clients. They also discuss the realities of hiring commission-based salespeople, whether AI can actually help generate quality B2B leads, and why the dream of passive income through memberships, courses, and e-commerce might be harder to achieve than some entrepreneurs think. items.desc: Gemini Decisions API Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million. Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio
items.full: 11th November 2026 - Link Blog Gemini Decisions API ( via ) Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million. Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. items.title: US corporate AI spending hits a new high in October, but growth slows to 1.65 percent
items.desc: According to the Ramp AI Index, US corporate AI spending rose just 1.65 percent in October 2026. One percent of companies still drive 80 percent of revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic. Customer support is emerging as a new growth driver, but it may bring lower margins than the coding business that has fueled spending so far. The article US corporate AI spending hits a new high in October, but growth slows to 1.65 percent appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: US corporate AI spending hit a new high in October 2026, but growth was modest. The Ramp AI Index, which tracks AI spending among business customers of financial services provider Ramp, showed a 1.65 percent increase month over month. The heaviest AI users spent somewhat more, according to Ramp . The top one percent of companies by AI spending paid a median of $10,200 per employee per month, up nine percent. A typical company, by contrast, spent just $16.32, a slight increase of less than a dollar from the previous month. Ad Ramp's data reflects market trends but isn't necessarily representative. The index draws on payment data from more than 85,000 US companies, though free AI tools and usage through personal accounts may be missing from the figures. Ad According to Ramp, separate metrics on token volume and spending come only from companies using Ramp Token Spend Management and aren't representative of overall AI spending on the platform. The customer base skews growth-oriented, tech-savvy, and larger than US businesses overall, so AI adoption is likely overstated. Business customers' spending on OpenAI grew 2.1 percent month over month, compared with just 0.5 percent for Anthropic. According to Ramp chief economist Ara Kharazian, the structural risks he identified in his earlier analysis persist. One percent of companies drive 80 percent of revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic. Ad That top tier is mostly venture-backed firms in tech, finance, and technical services. Outside those sectors, AI adoption is barely spreading. Prices are falling at the same time. The average price per million processed text tokens dropped 21 percent last month, according to Ramp. Usage volume is growing faster than spending, so AI keeps getting cheaper, driven by competitive pressure between OpenAI and Anthropic along with open-weight models from China. Ad SpacexSI also grew strongly at 2.2 percent, making it the fastest-growing software company in Ramp's entire dataset. That likely says more about bias in Ramp's data than about any big win for Grok. The company's models aren't particularly noteworthy, and the growth is probably driven by the coding tool Cursor, which belongs to SpacexSI . On Ramp, the company holds a 6.3 percent market share, a figure that most likely doesn't reflect the broader market. Anthropic reached 44.8 percent adoption, up 1.1 percentage points, while OpenAI held steady at 40.6 percent. Overall adoption of AI services rose to 56.8 percent. Software development teams accounted for 72 percent of all tracked AI spending in October, but their spending has declined from summer highs. Customer support and customer success departments saw the strongest growth, with their share of AI spending climbing from 0.8 percent in June to 13.3 percent in October, possibly driven by AI chatbots in customer service. Leadership teams also spent slightly more. But customer support is nowhere near matching the rapid growth development teams posted earlier this year, Kharazian writes. items.title: Google Deepmind's AlphaProof Code verified Signal's cryptographic core in four weeks instead of years
items.desc: Google Deepmind's AlphaProof Code mathematically verified Signal's cryptographic core code in four weeks, a process that typically takes years. AI agents powered by Gemini Carbon wrote more than six million lines of proof code and flagged only about one percent for human review. Deepmind plans to extend the method to critical infrastructure like power grids and medical devices. The article Google Deepmind's AlphaProof Code verified Signal's cryptographic core in four weeks instead of years appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Google Deepmind has unveiled AlphaProof Code, an AI system that mathematically proves software meets its security specs without errors. Researchers demonstrated the technology on Signal's encryption protocol, completing in four weeks work that typically takes years. Earlier verification efforts stopped at the theoretical design stage, according to a blog post by DeepMind researchers Pushmeet Kohli and Swarat Chaudhuri. AlphaProof Code verified the actual cryptographic core code running on users' devices. After experts defined formal security requirements, AI agents built on Gemini Carbon wrote over six million lines in the Lean proof language, flagging roughly one percent of the codebase for human review. Two bugs planted deliberately for testing were caught immediately. Signal CTO Ehren Kret says the approach strengthens trust in data privacy as AI threats grow. DeepMind plans to extend the method to power grids and medical devices through systems like CodeMender . items.title: Anthropic says AI is eroding Nvidia's CUDA lead, cutting an AMD chip switch from months to three days
items.desc: Anthropic claims it used AI itself to breach Nvidia's CUDA moat. The company's in-house model Mythos reportedly ported Claude to AMD GPUs in just three days, with almost no human intervention. Anthropic now runs Claude on four chip families and aims to cut costs and reduce vendor dependencies. The article Anthropic says AI is eroding Nvidia's CUDA lead, cutting an AMD chip switch from months to three days appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Anthropic claims it has broken free of its Nvidia dependence with a multi-chip strategy. The company says it ported its own AI model, Claude, to AMD GPUs in just three days, with almost no human intervention. Nvidia's biggest competitive edge is the combination of hardware and software, specifically CUDA, the software ecosystem that locks developers into Nvidia chips. Porting AI models to other chip architectures takes so much effort that many companies won't even try. Anthropic now claims in an investor presentation that it has solved this problem using AI itself. According to Tom Brown, co-founder and Chief Compute Officer at Anthropic, the company now trains and runs Claude on all four major chip families. Anthropic made an "unconventional bet" on a multi-chip strategy early on, at a time when most of the industry considered the effort not worth it. Each chip needs its own custom software and inference stack, which is expensive and time-consuming. But Anthropic has been investing in this work for years and has since become "incredibly good" at it, Brown says. Ad The company's most concrete test came with AMD GPUs. Until now, bringing up a new chip platform kept dozens of engineers busy for months. This year, Anthropic used AMD GPUs for the first time and let its own frontier model, Mythos, do the work. According to Anthropic, Claude was running on AMD after just three days, with almost no human intervention. The model ported or wrote nearly 100 percent of the kernels itself. Ad If these figures are accurate, the software overhead, long considered Nvidia's strongest competitive advantage, would shrink dramatically because of AI. Companies could switch more easily between chip providers and pick the most affordable or readily available option. In a compute market where supply is tight, a multi-chip approach lets companies focus on the best price-performance ratio, regardless of the vendor. Some chips are better for training, while others are better for inference. And because of its dominance in the AI chip market, Nvidia currently enjoys a margin of more than 70 percent, which is unusually high for hardware. Ad Anthropic treats compute from different vendors, chip architectures, and locations as one interchangeable pool. The company says it gets more out of every dollar of compute than any other frontier AI lab. Beyond its multi-chip strategy, Anthropic relies on what it calls compute multipliers, research breakthroughs that squeeze more performance from the same physical computing capacity. According to Anthropic, these multipliers build on one another so that each new breakthrough amplifies the effect of the previous one. Ad Eventually, Claude should be able to discover such compute multipliers on its own. That would amount to recursive self-improvement, a concept that's intensely debated in AI research but hasn't been proven yet . Ad Anthropic is also building its own data center capacity through the "Anthropic Direct" program. Instead of buying computing power only as a cloud service, the company leases chips and operates them in purpose-built data centers. The goal is to reduce total cost of ownership. items.desc: Do you want to make informed decisions to grow your website traffic, conversions, and revenue? Your website’s Google data (Search Console, Analytics, and Google Ads) tells you how your website is performing. But it doesn’t tell you why, or what you should do next. In…
items.full: Do you want to make informed decisions to grow your website traffic, conversions, and revenue? Your website’s Google data (Search Console, Analytics, and Google Ads) tells you how your website is performing. But it doesn’t tell you why, or what you should do next. In theory, connecting your data to AI should help you make informed decisions. The reality is that most AI connectors pass along raw data to AI without context. As a result, you get answers that sound confident, but you can’t differentiate real insights from invented ones. It simply shouldn’t be this hard to make informed decisions from your data. That’s why today, I’m really excited to introduce MeasureScale , a tool that connects your Google data to the AI assistant you already use. Website owners have been telling us for a while that they don’t trust the answers AI gives them about their data. Many end up double-checking every number by hand, which defeats the whole point. So we built MeasureScale to fix it. MeasureScale is an MCP server that connects your AI assistants to Google Search Console, Google Analytics, and Google Ads. MCP stands for Model Context Protocol, which is the open standard that lets AI assistants connect to external tools and data. Here is what makes MeasureScale special: Instead of passing along raw data to AI without context, MeasureScale picks the analysis first based on your question and runs it on your live data. Your AI then gets the finished analysis and turns it into a plain answer to your questions. MeasureScale works with Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Cursor, Claude Code, and any other app that supports MCP. Best of all, there’s nothing to install on your website. It works with any site verified in Google Search Console, whether it runs on WordPress or not. The biggest problem with asking AI about your data is trust. How do you know the insights it just gave you are real? MeasureScale solves this by showing the source. Every answer tells you which data source it came from, which dates it covers, and whether the data is final yet. If Google Search Console only returned part of your data, the answer says so. If Google Analytics sampled a report, you’ll know that too. This way, you never mistake an estimate for a fact. Let’s look at how MeasureScale helps you make informed decisions with your Search Console, Analytics, and Ads data. Google Search Console shows how people find your site on Google. MeasureScale turns that data into a clear plan for growing your traffic. A good place to start is quick wins. Some of your easiest traffic gains are already hiding in your data. These are searches where your pages rank just off the first page of Google. MeasureScale finds these “striking distance” keywords for you. It then estimates how many extra clicks each one could bring, based on your own site’s click-through rates instead of industry averages. For example, you can ask, “Which searches are close to page one?” You’ll get a ranked list of pages to improve first, along with the clicks each one could earn.
